docs.title: Session 06: Copilot Spaces & Context Management
docs.text:
Launch Slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Copilot in Practice Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions 01 to 05 Duration: 3 hours (1 hr trainer content + 2 hr lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Give Copilot the context a task needs. Learners use one Storefront API to select Space sources, add repository instructions, compare context levels, and store reusable prompts.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
• Create Copilot Spaces for team workflows
  • Write project-level and user-level custom instructions
  • Create reusable prompt files for team standards
  • Explain how instructions, Spaces, and Memory work together
  • Review and update context as a project changes
  • Choose the smallest source set that supports a task and verify claims against it

docs.title: Session Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Lab exercises lab/ Lab starter files lab/starter/ Lab solution files lab/solution/

docs.title: Key Topics
docs.text:
• Copilot Spaces: selected context sources
  • .github/copilot-instructions.md: project-level instructions
  • .github/prompts/*.md: reusable prompt files
  • VS Code instruction settings
  • Context selection as a policy-approved workflow
  • Before/after context comparison

docs.title: Give each task the repository evidence it needs
Access and cost preflight
docs.text:
Follow the course safety baseline.

  1. Check the current GitHub docs and your organization's rules.
  2. Check the repository and data sources.
  3. Use a small question and synthetic data.
  4. Set a usage limit for metered work.

docs.title: Context selection
docs.text:
Choose evidence a reviewer can explain:

  • repository instructions;
  • relevant source files and tests;
  • architecture or API documents;
  • approved task notes.

Do not include unapproved data merely to make a prompt more complete.

docs.title: Context packet exercise
docs.text:
Task: add validation to an API endpoint

Packet:
- route file
- corresponding tests
- API contract
- repository conventions

Ask learners to explain why each source is needed and what is excluded.

docs.title: Evaluate the result
docs.text:
• Does it cite or follow the selected repository evidence?
  • Is the scope limited to the task?
  • Are assumptions surfaced for human review?
  • Do relevant tests pass?

docs.title: Required access
docs.text: Confirm Spaces and GitHub Copilot access before the lab. If either is unavailable, stop the lab. A manually assembled packet does not demonstrate Space creation, reuse, or behavior.

docs.title: Agenda and time plan
docs.text:
Time Topic Trainer move 0:00 Why context fails Diagnose a vague response 0:08 Context layers Build a source hierarchy 0:18 Spaces Curate and share evidence 0:30 Instructions and prompt files Show repository artifacts 0:42 Memory and maintenance Separate preview from policy 0:50 Before/after demo Compare with a rubric 0:58 Lab handoff Assign context packet

Transition: "Better output begins with better evidence, not a longer prompt."

docs.title: The context problem
docs.text:
Copilot cannot reliably apply information it cannot see. Extra context can create noise or expose data unnecessarily.

Common failure modes:

  • the relevant contract is absent;
  • stale documentation conflicts with source code;
  • broad context hides the key constraint;
  • local preferences are mistaken for team standards;
  • restricted data is included without approval.

Context selection is an engineering and governance decision. Keep the packet focused.

docs.title: A practical context hierarchy
docs.text:
Task intent and acceptance criteria
               ↓
Repository instructions and prompt workflow
               ↓
Curated Space: code, docs, issues, specifications
               ↓
Current file and explicit references
               ↓
Validated memory, when supported and approved

Specific task constraints override generic guidance. Clarify conflicts.

docs.title: Copilot Spaces
docs.text:
A Space is a selected set of sources for a recurring topic or workflow.

Good candidates include:

  • source repositories and key paths;
  • architecture and API documentation;
  • approved issues and specifications;
  • team guidance for a domain;
  • links whose ownership and freshness are known.

Do not use a Space to collect restricted information without approval.

docs.title: Curate for a purpose
docs.text:
Space: Storefront API
├── API specification
├── product route and model
├── architecture note
├── error-handling conventions
└── repository instructions

Exclude unrelated services, production data, secrets, abandoned proposals, and documents with no accountable owner.

Trainer cue: Ask learners what they would remove first if the answer became noisy.

docs.title: Sharing Spaces safely
docs.text:
Before sharing:

  1. Name the intended audience and task.
  2. Confirm every source is approved for that audience.
  3. Add purpose-specific instructions.
  4. Assign an owner and review date.
  5. Test with a known question and compare against source evidence.
  6. Remove or replace stale sources.

Current access controls and sharing behavior must be verified before the demo.

docs.title: Repository-level instructions
docs.text:
Create .github/copilot-instructions.md for durable project guidance:

# Repository guidance

- Use TypeScript strict mode.
- Validate request input at the route boundary.
- Keep business logic in `src/services/`.
- Run `npm test` before proposing completion.
- Do not add dependencies without reviewer approval.

Write rules that can be observed. Avoid vague goals such as "produce high-quality code."

docs.title: Reusable prompt files
docs.text:
Place team-reviewed workflows under .github/prompts/:

---
description: Review an API change against its contract
---

Read the selected route, service, tests, and API contract.
List mismatches before suggesting changes.
Do not edit files outside the selected feature.
End with the focused validation command.

Verify the current supported filename and frontmatter behavior before delivery.

docs.title: VS Code instruction settings
docs.text:
The curriculum references:

{
  "github.copilot.chat.codeGeneration.useInstructionFiles": true
}

Treat settings as version-sensitive:

  • verify current documentation and the learner's IDE version;
  • show where workspace settings are reviewed;
  • do not claim an instruction loaded without observing the result;
  • retain the instructions as a useful manual checklist.

docs.title: Copilot Memory
docs.text:
Memory may let an agent retain and validate useful knowledge, depending on support and approval.

Use three questions:

  1. Source: Where did this fact come from?
  2. Scope: Does it apply to this user, repository, or task?
  3. Freshness: How will it be corrected when the code changes?

Never store secrets, restricted data, or guesses. Verify current availability and controls.

docs.title: Demo: without grounded context
docs.text:
Prompt:

Add a low-stock report endpoint.

Expected discussion:

  • Which endpoint?
  • Which inputs and error schema?
  • Where is validation normally performed?
  • Which tests prove the behavior?
  • Which data is safe to include?

Do not score the response by confidence or length.

docs.title: Demo: with a context packet
docs.text:
Using the Storefront API specification, product route, product model, architecture
note, and repository instructions, propose the smallest low-stock endpoint change.

First list acceptance criteria and assumptions. Do not add dependencies.
End with two verification requests and cite the evidence used.

Compare outputs for correctness, scope, assumptions, evidence, and testability.

docs.title: Concrete code target
docs.text:
function parseThreshold(value) {
  if (value === undefined) return 10;
  if (!/^\d+$/.test(value)) {
    throw new Error("threshold must be a non-negative integer");
  }
  return Number(value);
}

Ask where the static report route must appear relative to /:id. The correct next action may be clarification rather than code generation.

docs.title: Maintenance is part of context
docs.text:
Trigger Maintenance action API contract changes Update Space sources and prompts Repository convention changes Review instruction files Ownership changes Assign a new maintainer Output contradicts source Remove stale evidence and retest Feature behavior changes Recheck official documentation

Schedule reviews; do not wait for failures.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Learners will:

  1. keep one Storefront API for the full lab;
  2. select the smallest approved source set;
  3. add repository instructions and a low-stock endpoint;
  4. compare one logging task across context levels;
  5. store and test three reusable prompt files.

Final deliverable: A reviewable Storefront API context package with comparison and verification evidence.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Relevant context matters more than a large context packet.
  2. Spaces curate evidence for a purpose and audience.
  3. Instructions encode durable rules; prompt files encode reusable tasks.
  4. Memory requires source, scope, freshness, and current policy checks.
  5. Every context source needs an owner and maintenance path.

docs.title: Questions and lab readiness
docs.text:
Which source would you remove from a context packet, and why?

  • Which source is authoritative?
  • What must stay out of the Space?
  • Who will maintain the resulting artifacts?

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session 06 Lab: Spaces and Context Management
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions 01 to 05 completed Deliverable: A context package for one Storefront API, with comparison evidence

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
Use one Storefront API for the full lab. First select the sources for a Copilot Space. Then add repository instructions and compare the same task across context levels. Store reusable prompt files beside the project.

Stage Work Time 1 Prepare the project and select Space sources 30 min 2 Add repository instructions 30 min 3 Compare one task across context levels 30 min 4 Build and test a prompt library 30 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Read the course safety baseline. Use only the synthetic Storefront API files supplied with this lab.

You need:

  • required GitHub Copilot access in the editor;
  • Copilot Spaces access if you will use the live Space path;
  • a repository or approved sandbox that can hold the Storefront API;
  • Node.js and npm;
  • permission to add repository instructions and prompt files.

If Copilot Spaces or GitHub Copilot is unavailable, stop the lab. A local context packet can support later review, but it does not replace creating and testing a Space.

Create a writable copy:

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-06
cp -R sessions/session-06-spaces-and-context/lab/starter/ecommerce-project \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-06/storefront-api
cp sessions/session-06-spaces-and-context/lab/starter/context-comparison.md \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-06/storefront-api/
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-06/storefront-api
npm install
npm start

Open http://localhost:3000/api/products. The response should contain the seeded products.

docs.title: Stage 1: Prepare the project and select Space sources (30 minutes)
Inspect the context before adding it
docs.text:
Read these files:

Source Decision it supports README.md Project purpose, setup, and endpoints docs/api-spec.md Required HTTP behavior docs/architecture.md Layers, response envelopes, and naming src/models/product.js Product fields and validation src/routes/products.js Current route patterns

Write context-notes.md:

# Storefront API Context Notes

## Task
Add a low-stock report endpoint.

## Required sources
## Excluded sources
## Conflicts or stale statements
## Acceptance criteria

For this task, keep the source set small. Do not add unrelated repositories, private discussions, or production data.

docs.title: Live Space path
docs.text:
Create a Space named Storefront API Lab. Add the five reviewed files and these instructions:

Answer from the selected Storefront API sources. Follow docs/api-spec.md and
docs/architecture.md. Use the Product validation and response patterns already in
the project. State when a requested behavior is not defined by the sources.

Ask:

What files and acceptance criteria should guide a low-stock report endpoint?
Do not write code yet.

Verify every claim against the selected sources.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1: context scope is visible
docs.text:
• context-notes.md names the task and acceptance criteria.
  • Every selected source has a reason to be present.
  • Unrelated or restricted sources are excluded.
  • Claims in the first answer trace to a selected file.
  • The live Space or local context packet is ready for reuse.

docs.title: Stage 2: Add repository instructions (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Create .github/copilot-instructions.md in the Storefront API:

# Storefront API Instructions

- Use ES modules.
- Keep route handlers under `src/routes/`.
- Follow the `{ data: ... }` success envelope.
- Return errors as `{ error: { code, message, details? } }`.
- Use `Product.validate()` before product data changes.
- Add no dependency unless the task requires it and a reviewer approves it.
- Keep examples and tests on synthetic data.

Ask Copilot to plan the low-stock endpoint:

Plan a GET /api/products/reports/low-stock endpoint for this project. It should
accept an optional non-negative integer threshold and default to 10. Return only
products whose stock is at or below the threshold. Follow repository instructions.
Do not edit files.

Review the plan against the API spec, architecture, model, and existing route order. A static route must not be hidden behind /:id.

Then ask for a minimal implementation and verification:

Implement the accepted low-stock endpoint plan. Keep the current API behavior.
Run the smallest useful check and show the result.

Manually verify:

curl "http://localhost:3000/api/products/reports/low-stock?threshold=80"
curl "http://localhost:3000/api/products/reports/low-stock?threshold=-1"

Compare your instruction file with lab/solution/ecommerce-project/.github/copilot-instructions.md.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2: instructions changed observable behavior
docs.text:
• The plan uses ES modules and existing response envelopes.
  • The route is placed before /:id.
  • Invalid thresholds produce a structured 400 response.
  • Existing product routes still work.
  • context-notes.md records one instruction Copilot followed and one item you still had to review.

docs.title: Stage 3: Compare one task across context levels (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Open context-comparison.md. Use the same task in every experiment:

Add request-logging middleware to the Storefront API. Record timestamp, method,
URL, response time, and status code. Use info for 2xx, warn for 4xx, and error for
5xx. Add no logging package.

Run four experiments without changing the task:

  1. No project context: Ask from an empty window.
  2. Repository context: Open the Storefront API with copilot-instructions.md.
  3. Space or context packet: Ask with the selected project sources.
  4. Prompt file: Use a structured repository prompt for the task.

Record:

  • import style;
  • file placement;
  • response and error conventions;
  • added assumptions;
  • number of corrections;
  • claims that cite or clearly follow a source.

Score usefulness against the project, not fluency. More context is only better when it removes wrong assumptions.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3: comparison uses evidence
docs.text:
• All four experiments use the same task text.
  • Each score cites a concrete output difference.
  • The comparison identifies one useful source and one source that added no value.
  • The final choice states the smallest context set that supports the task.

docs.title: Stage 4: Build and test a prompt library (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Create these files in storefront-api/.github/prompts/:

  1. investigate-bug.prompt.md
  2. generate-api-docs.prompt.md
  3. migration-checklist.prompt.md

Each prompt needs front matter with a short description, a bounded input, expected output sections, and a verification step.

docs.title: Test the prompts on the same project
docs.text:
• Run investigate-bug against an invalid minPrice query scenario.
  • Run generate-api-docs against the low-stock endpoint.
  • Run migration-checklist for a proposed Express major-version update. Do not install it.

Review each result:

  • Did it stay inside the selected Storefront API sources?
  • Did it separate known facts from assumptions?
  • Did it name a check another engineer can run?
  • Did it avoid changing code when the prompt only requested analysis?

Compare with lab/solution/ecommerce-project/.github/prompts/.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4: prompts are reusable and bounded
docs.text:
• All three prompt files appear in .github/prompts/.
  • Each prompt was tested on the Storefront API.
  • Each output includes verification.
  • The migration prompt stops before package changes.
  • Stale or duplicate instructions were removed.

docs.title: Final Deliverable
docs.text:
Submit the storefront-api/ workspace with:

  1. context-notes.md and either the Space source list or context-packet.md.
  2. .github/copilot-instructions.md.
  3. The completed context-comparison.md.
  4. Three tested prompt files under .github/prompts/.
  5. Low-stock endpoint verification and the final context choice.

Done: Another engineer can see which sources were selected, how each context layer changed the result, and how to verify the project-specific output.

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session 06: Context Workflows
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Delivery baseline
docs.text: Read the course safety baseline. Before the demo, check the current GitHub docs and your organization's rules. Product behavior and availability can change.

docs.title: Access and cost preflight
docs.text:
1. Choose the training repository and synthetic data.
  2. Check which sources learners may add or share.
  3. Choose a small question and the files needed to answer it.
  4. Set a usage limit if the work is metered.
  5. Check Spaces and GitHub Copilot access before the lab.

docs.title: Access failure
docs.text: Stop the learner lab. A printed context packet may support the trainer demonstration, but it does not count as learner completion.

docs.title: Session objective
docs.text: Teach learners to select the few files needed for a task and check the answer against those files.

docs.title: Suggested agenda
docs.text: Segment Activity Preflight Check data, sources, usage limits, and access. Source selection Select only relevant repository instructions, code, tests, and docs. Context packet Explain why every included source is necessary. Small task Use the packet to plan a small change. Review Check the output against the source files and tests. Access gate Stop when required Spaces or Copilot access is missing.

docs.title: Context packet pattern
docs.text:
Task: make one API behavior change

Include:
- route or service file
- focused tests
- relevant API contract
- repository conventions

Exclude:
- unrelated repositories
- sensitive data
- broad documentation that does not affect the task

docs.title: Trainer talking points
docs.text:
"Select the fewest files needed to explain and check the result."

"If source eligibility or product behavior is unclear, stop and resolve the access or policy question before the lab."

"For metered work, stop at the usage limit."

docs.title: Review rubric
docs.text:
• Does every source have a clear relationship to the task?
  • Is all included data allowed for the lab?
  • Does the result follow the source files and acceptance criteria?
  • Are assumptions identified for human review?
  • Can the task be completed manually from the packet?

docs.title: Close
docs.text: Ask learners to identify a task that would be easier to review with fewer files.

docs.title: Minute-mapped delivery plan (60 minutes)
docs.text: Time Segment Trainer outcome 0:00 to 0:08 Diagnose the context problem Learners distinguish missing information from excess noise. 0:08 to 0:18 Context hierarchy Learners rank task, instructions, curated sources, and local references. 0:18 to 0:30 Curated context workflows The group creates a purpose, audience, source list, and owner. 0:30 to 0:42 Instructions and reusable prompts Learners separate durable rules from repeatable tasks. 0:42 to 0:50 Source governance and maintenance Each source receives scope and freshness checks. 0:50 to 0:58 Scripted before/after demo The group compares two responses with the source files. 0:58 to 1:00 Close and lab handoff Learners begin with the context packet.

docs.title: Time-pressure cutpoints
docs.text:
• At 0:08, use one missing-context and one excess-context example.
  • At 0:18, keep the hierarchy diagram and omit secondary surface examples.
  • At 0:30, describe sharing rather than navigating a changing UI.
  • At 0:42, create one instruction excerpt and one prompt file, not a library.
  • At 0:50, mention memory only as an availability-dependent concept requiring verification.
  • At 0:55, compare plans rather than waiting for generated code.
  • Never cut source approval, maintenance ownership, access checks, or lab boundaries.

docs.title: Trainer talking points
docs.text:
• Context is an engineering input. It does not authorize collecting everything available.
  • Missing contracts cause invented assumptions.
  • Broad, stale, or conflicting sources can obscure the decisive rule.
  • Restricted data must not be added merely because it seems relevant.
  • A confident answer is not evidence that the right source was used.
  • The lasting skill is selecting the fewest files needed for review.

docs.title: Opening exercise
docs.text:
Display this request:

Add validation to the checkout endpoint.

Ask learners what is missing.

Expected answers include endpoint location, input contract, error shape, repository conventions, focused tests, and allowed data.

Then ask what should not be added.

Expected answers include unrelated repositories, production records, secrets, and ownerless stale documents.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "We can organize those choices as a hierarchy, starting with the task itself."

docs.title: Detailed talking points
docs.text:
1. Task intent and acceptance criteria define the immediate outcome.
  2. Repository instructions provide durable, reviewed conventions.
  3. Reusable prompt files encode repeatable workflows.
  4. Curated collections can bring code, docs, issues, and specifications together.
  5. Current files and named references supply local context.
  6. Retained memory needs a source, scope, and review date.
  7. Specific task requirements override generic guidance.
  8. Conflicts require clarification; they are not resolved by adding more context.

docs.title: Source-ranking exercise
docs.text:
For a fictional quantity-validation change, rank:

  • current API contract;
  • focused route tests;
  • owned architecture note;
  • unrelated product roadmap;
  • production request log.

Include the contract, tests, and the relevant owned note.

Exclude the unrelated roadmap and production log.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "A useful curated workflow makes that source decision explicit and maintainable."

docs.title: Access and governance check
docs.text:
1. Revisit the Delivery baseline.
  2. Check the current GitHub docs for Spaces.
  3. Check repository access and use only synthetic data.
  4. Check the rules for adding and sharing sources.
  5. Set a usage limit and name who can approve more.
  6. Stop if the required sources are missing.

docs.title: Trainer-created context card
docs.text:
Purpose: answer questions about the fictional Checkout API validation behavior.
Audience: workshop participants.
Owner: training repository maintainer.
Review date: before the next cohort.

Include:
- docs/api-contract.md
- src/routes/checkout.ts
- src/services/checkout.ts
- tests/checkout.test.ts
- .github/copilot-instructions.md

Exclude:
- production data
- secrets and credentials
- unrelated services
- abandoned proposals

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
• A curated Space may support this workflow when it is available and approved.
  • Do not infer sharing, access, retention, or entitlement behavior.
  • Verify those facts in current official documentation and organizational policy.
  • Source-level access does not automatically authorize a new audience or use.
  • Assign an owner and review trigger before sharing.
  • Test the packet with a known question whose answer exists in the sources.

docs.title: Observable outcome
docs.text: Learners can explain why every included source is necessary and why every excluded source is unnecessary or unsuitable.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Curated evidence answers what the project says; repository instructions state how work should proceed."

docs.title: Segment 4: Instructions and reusable prompts (0:30 to 0:42)
Repository instruction example
docs.text:
# Repository guidance

- Validate request input at the route boundary.
- Keep business logic in src/services/.
- Preserve the documented error response shape.
- Run the focused test before proposing completion.
- Do not add dependencies without reviewer approval.

docs.title: Trainer talking points
docs.text:
• Use observable instructions rather than "write high-quality code."
  • Keep durable conventions separate from one feature's requirements.
  • Review instruction files through the repository's normal process.
  • Instructions guide proposals; they are not enforcement or proof.
  • Verify current supported paths, names, and settings before demonstrating.
  • Retain the text as a manual checklist if loading behavior is unavailable.

docs.title: Reusable prompt example
docs.text:
---
description: Review a low-stock endpoint change
---

Read the selected contract, route, service, tests, and repository guidance.
List mismatches before proposing changes.
Do not edit files outside the selected feature.
End with assumptions, cited evidence, and the focused validation command.

docs.title: Pair exercise
docs.text:
Ask pairs to label each sentence as:

  • durable instruction;
  • task-specific prompt;
  • acceptance criterion;
  • unsuitable vague guidance.

Debrief disagreements and move feature-specific behavior out of repository-wide rules.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Context is useful only while its source, scope, and freshness remain trustworthy."

docs.title: Segment 5: Source governance and maintenance (0:42 to 0:50)
Three-question check
docs.text:
For every source or remembered fact, ask:

  1. Source: Where did this fact come from?
  2. Scope: Which repository, audience, and task does it apply to?
  3. Freshness: Which event or date triggers revalidation?

docs.title: Maintenance table
docs.text: Trigger Required action API contract changes Update packet sources and retest a known question. Repository convention changes Review instruction and prompt files. Source owner changes Assign a new accountable maintainer. Output conflicts with evidence Remove stale sources and clarify authority. Product behavior changes Recheck current official documentation. Policy or audience changes Reapprove source eligibility and sharing.

docs.title: Safe delivery wording
docs.text: "Availability-dependent memory or context features must be verified before use. Never store secrets, restricted material, or guesses. The manual source log remains authoritative for this exercise."

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "We will now test whether a smaller grounded packet produces a more reviewable plan."

docs.title: Scripted demo: Low-stock reporting with and without grounding (0:50 to 0:58)
Purpose
docs.text: Compare the responses against clear criteria. Do not claim that a product surface always cites or follows context.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Use four excerpts from the Storefront API lab:

docs/api-spec.md:

Product list responses use the existing data envelope.
Invalid query values use the existing VALIDATION_ERROR response.

src/routes/products.js:

router.get('/:id', async (req, res) => {
  // Existing dynamic route.
});

src/models/product.js defines product stock as a non-negative integer.

The lab task requires GET /api/products/reports/low-stock, an optional non-negative integer threshold, and a default threshold of 10.

Use synthetic data only.

docs.title: Pass A: Minimal prompt
docs.text:
Exact prompt:

Add a low-stock report endpoint.

docs.title: Trainer actions for Pass A
docs.text:
1. If approved access exists, submit the prompt without project context.
  2. Otherwise reveal a prepared generic proposal.
  3. Record assumptions about the route, threshold, error shape, and test command.
  4. Do not score writing style or confidence.

docs.title: Expected observation for Pass A
docs.text:
The response may place the route after /:id, accept invalid thresholds, invent an error, or omit verification.

Variation is acceptable; the teaching point is that the request lacks evidence.

docs.title: Exact trainer prompt
docs.text:
Exact prompt:

Using only the API specification, product route, product model, and
repository instructions, propose the smallest low-stock endpoint change.
First list acceptance criteria and assumptions.
Do not add dependencies. Reject negative or non-integer thresholds.
End with the source files used and two checks to run.

docs.title: Exact trainer actions for Pass B
docs.text:
1. Check that each source is current and allowed for the lab.
  2. Submit through the context workflow.
  3. Require acceptance criteria before code.
  4. Compare the plan with the API specification and route order.
  5. Ask whether Number.isInteger(Number(value)) would wrongly accept "2".
  6. Check the default and invalid threshold paths.
  7. Record any unsupported assumption.

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text:
The grounded response should state the threshold rules, place the static route before /:id, avoid new dependencies, name its source files, and list two checks.

It may then include a code proposal such as:

function parseThreshold(value) {
  if (value === undefined) return 10;
  if (!/^\d+$/.test(value)) {
    throw new Error('threshold must be a non-negative integer');
  }
  return Number(value);
}

Check the existing project before choosing the error type and message.

docs.title: Verification rubric
docs.text: Dimension Pass question Correctness Are the default, valid, and invalid threshold paths represented? Scope Is the proposal limited to the selected feature? Assumptions Are unresolved decisions named? Sources Can each behavior be traced to a source file? Testability Are valid and invalid cases clear? Data Was only synthetic data used?

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
Give half the room only the minimal request.

Give the other half the four-source packet and grounded prompt.

Each group writes a plan, not code.

Swap plans and score them with the rubric.

Reveal the code proposal only during debrief. Use this to recover the trainer demonstration, not as a learner substitute.

docs.title: Demo recovery
docs.text:
• If the surface is unavailable during the demonstration, use the printed responses and fix access before the lab.
  • If it ignores an instruction, mark the mismatch; do not claim enforcement.
  • If sources conflict, stop and assign clarification to the source owner.
  • If the packet is noisy, remove one source and explain the decision.
  • If time expires, compare acceptance criteria and skip code generation.

docs.title: "Should we add the whole repository?"
docs.text: No. Start with the fewest files that support the task, then add a file only when the answer is missing specific information.

docs.title: "Do instructions guarantee compliance?"
docs.text: No. They guide output. Tests, repository checks, and human review enforce the rules.

docs.title: "Which source wins when docs and code disagree?"
docs.text: Do not guess. Identify the accountable source owner, record the conflict, and clarify before implementation.

docs.title: "Can we include issue comments or meeting notes?"
docs.text: Only when the lab permits them and they are relevant, owned, and current. Separate decisions from unverified discussion.

docs.title: "Does a Space change repository permissions?"
docs.text: Do not guess how access works. Check the current docs and organization rules before adding or sharing a source.

docs.title: "Can we store team conventions in memory?"
docs.text: Keep long-lived team rules in reviewed repository files. Before using a memory feature, check current support, data rules, sources, scope, and review dates.

docs.title: "Why did the grounded response still miss a rule?"
docs.text: Context supplies more information. It does not guarantee correct use. State the rule, test it, and review the result.

docs.title: "What does this cost?"
docs.text: Check current metering information and use the organization's usage limit.

docs.title: Pitfalls, anti-patterns, and recoveries
docs.text: Anti-pattern Recovery "More context is always better" Remove sources that do not affect a criterion. Adding restricted records Stop, remove them, notify the appropriate owner, and use synthetic data. Mixing stale and current contracts Identify authority and update or exclude the stale source. Vague instructions Rewrite them as behavior a test or reviewer can check. Treating citations as correctness Open the source and check the claim. No source owner Assign one or do not share the packet. No review date Add event-based and scheduled maintenance triggers. Assuming instructions loaded Test the expected behavior. Teaching fixed paths or UI Check current docs before delivery. Context changes without review Manage shared artifacts through normal repository review.

docs.title: Closing script
docs.text: "Good context is small enough to explain, safe to share, tied to source files, and maintained by an owner. Better output starts with better source decisions."

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Open lab/README.md.

Learners keep one Storefront API through source selection, repository instructions, a context comparison, and reusable prompts.

Check current support before using a changing UI, path, setting, sharing control, or memory feature.

docs.title: Readiness checklist
docs.text:
• Purpose, audience, and owner are written.
  • Every source is allowed for the lab and uses synthetic data.
  • Exclusions are clear.
  • One known-answer question is ready.
  • Maintenance triggers are assigned.
  • Required Spaces and GitHub Copilot access is confirmed.
  • A usage limit is recorded when it applies.

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session 07: Copilot for Code Review & Pull Requests
docs.text:
Launch Slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Copilot in Practice Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions 01 to 06 Duration: 3 hours (1 hr trainer content + 2 hr lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Follow one pull request from change brief to final human decision. Learners inspect a flawed change and compare human and Copilot findings. They correct the code, resolve a conflict, and record the evidence required for approval.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
• Use Copilot to generate PR summaries and review comments
  • Configure automatic Copilot reviews at repository or organization level
  • Evaluate Copilot review quality and blind spots
  • Resolve merge conflicts using the cloud agent
  • Add Copilot to a team code-review workflow
  • Tie every blocking comment and accepted fix to reproducible evidence

docs.title: Session Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Lab exercises lab/ Lab starter files lab/starter/ Lab solution files lab/solution/

docs.title: Key Topics
docs.text:
• PR summaries and commit message generation
  • Copilot code review, manual and automatic
  • Review comments with one-click fixes
  • Merge conflict resolution via cloud agent
  • Quality gates and team adoption

docs.title: Evidence, human judgment, and policy-approved automation
Access and cost preflight
docs.text:
Follow the course safety baseline.

  1. Check the current GitHub docs and your organization's rules.
  2. Check the repository, data, and review permissions.
  3. Use a small pull request with clear acceptance criteria.
  4. Set a usage limit for metered work.

docs.title: Review is a human responsibility
docs.text:
Automation may raise questions. A reviewer decides whether a change is correct, safe, maintainable, and within scope.

Issue and acceptance criteria
        ↓
Proposed change and checks
        ↓
Human review
        ↓
Accept, request revision, or implement manually

docs.title: Review rubric
docs.text:
• Correctness against acceptance criteria
  • Tests and validation evidence
  • Security, dependency, and permission implications
  • Scope and maintainability
  • Repository conventions and human approval

docs.title: Conflict-resolution exercise
docs.text:
1. Read both branch intentions.
  2. Write the merged behavior and tests before editing.
  3. Resolve the conflict manually in the repository sandbox.
  4. Run checks and request review.
  5. Demonstrate an approved assisted workflow only after checking current documentation and policy.

docs.title: Required access
docs.text: Confirm Copilot review, pull-request access, Git, Node.js, and npm before the lab. If a requirement is missing, stop and resolve it. A worksheet-only review does not replace the pull-request workflow.

docs.title: Agenda and time plan
docs.text:
Time Topic Trainer move 0:00 Review workflow and roles Define accountability 0:08 Summaries and descriptions Separate draft from evidence 0:18 Manual and automatic review Show policy controls 0:28 End-to-end PR demo Apply the rubric 0:43 Suggestions and conflicts Preserve author intent 0:51 Limits and adoption Design human gates 0:58 Lab handoff and Q&A Assign reviewer roles

Transition: "Copilot can increase review coverage; it cannot own the decision."

docs.title: Copilot across a PR lifecycle
docs.text:
Issue and acceptance criteria
          ↓
Branch and bounded commits
          ↓
Draft summary and PR description
          ↓
Automated checks + Copilot first pass
          ↓
Human review and author response
          ↓
Approval, revision, or close

Each stage gives the accountable reviewer evidence.

docs.title: Commit messages and PR descriptions
docs.text:
Copilot can draft text from the visible change, but authors must verify:

  • the user-visible behavior is accurate;
  • tests and results are not invented;
  • breaking changes and migrations are explicit;
  • security and dependency implications are named;
  • issue links and acceptance criteria match the work;
  • no sensitive details appear in generated prose.

A polished summary can still be wrong.

docs.title: A reviewable PR template
docs.text:
## Problem
What user-visible problem does this solve?

## Change
List the bounded implementation choices.

## Validation
- [ ] Focused tests
- [ ] Existing checks
- [ ] Manual edge case

## Risk and rollback
Name data, dependency, security, and recovery considerations.

docs.title: Requesting Copilot review
docs.text:
For a manual request:

  1. Confirm the PR is ready for a first pass.
  2. Verify current availability, permissions, and repository policy.
  3. Request the Copilot review through the supported PR control.
  4. Wait for comments and review them as hypotheses.
  5. Resolve, reject with rationale, or implement a verified fix.
  6. Request human review with the complete evidence.

Do not use Copilot review to bypass required reviewers.

docs.title: Automatic review configuration
docs.text:
Automatic review can be configured at repository or organization scope when supported.

Before enabling:

  • identify eligible repositories and excluded data;
  • define when reviews run and who owns triage;
  • preserve branch protection and required human approvals;
  • monitor noise, missed findings, and review delay;
  • document an off switch and escalation owner.

Trainer cue: Demonstrate navigation, not fixed UI labels that may change.

docs.title: Quality gates
docs.text:
Gate Evidence Ready for first pass Clear description, focused diff, tests available Ready for human review Checks pass; AI comments triaged Ready for approval Acceptance criteria met; risks reviewed Ready for merge Required approvals and branch protections satisfied

Copilot review comes before human approval. It never replaces it.

docs.title: Demo PR: intentional defect
docs.text:
export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}

The requirement says suspended users must never view invoices.

if (user.status === "suspended") return false;
return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;

Ask which tests and policy evidence should accompany this suggestion.

docs.title: Demo narrative: complete lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Open the issue and read acceptance criteria aloud.
  2. Inspect the focused branch diff before generated prose.
  3. Generate or improve the PR description; correct unsupported claims.
  4. Run required checks and request Copilot review.
  5. Classify each comment: valid, uncertain, noise, or out of scope.
  6. Apply one verified fix and add a regression test.
  7. Request human review and record the final decision.

docs.title: Reviewing suggested fixes
docs.text:
Before applying:

  • restate the finding in your own words;
  • reproduce the defect or identify the violated requirement;
  • inspect the complete patch, not only highlighted lines;
  • add or update a test that fails before the fix;
  • run broader checks appropriate to the risk;
  • retain author ownership of the resulting code.

One-click application saves typing. The reviewer still decides.

docs.title: What review may catch
docs.text:
• localized correctness issues;
  • missing error handling or tests;
  • suspicious patterns visible in the diff;
  • inconsistent naming or repository conventions;
  • simple maintainability concerns.

docs.title: What it may miss
docs.text:
• unstated product intent;
  • cross-system behavior absent from context;
  • runtime, operational, legal, or organizational risk;
  • subtle authorization and data-boundary flaws;
  • deliberately misleading but plausible changes.

docs.title: Merge conflict resolution
docs.text:
Base behavior + branch A intent + branch B intent
                        ↓
              write merged acceptance criteria
                        ↓
                resolve conflict in sandbox
                        ↓
                 run tests and human review

If an approved cloud-agent workflow is available, compare its proposal with the manual resolution. Do not blindly choose "ours" or "theirs."

docs.title: Adoption patterns
docs.text:
Start: Optional first-pass review on a small set of repositories.

Measure: Actionable findings, false positives, review time, rework, and defects that reach users.

Adapt: Tune scope, guidance, ownership, and escalation.

Expand: Only when quality, security, and developer experience meet team criteria.

Keep a documented pause or disable path for unavailable features and exceptional repositories.

docs.title: Facilitation prompts
docs.text:
• Which comment needs domain expertise to evaluate?
  • What evidence would turn an uncertain comment into a decision?
  • Who resolves review noise?
  • Which repositories should not use automatic review?
  • How will the team detect over-reliance?

Transition: "Now apply the workflow as both author and reviewer."

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Learners will:

  1. follow one pull request from a flawed change brief;
  2. classify human and Copilot findings;
  3. apply only fixes supported by evidence;
  4. resolve the prepared conflict without losing either branch goal;
  5. make an explicit final human decision.

Final deliverable: Review notes, the corrected project, conflict results, and the final decision.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Generated summaries must be verified against the diff.
  2. AI review is a first pass before accountable human review.
  3. Suggested fixes require reproduction, inspection, and tests.
  4. Conflict resolution starts from intended merged behavior.
  5. Adoption should be measured and reversible.

docs.title: Questions and lab readiness
docs.text:
Which review decision must never be delegated without human evidence?

  • Who is the final reviewer?
  • Which check is required before requesting review?
  • Is the conflict scenario ready?

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session 07 Lab: Code Review Workflows
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions 01 to 06 completed Deliverable: A human-reviewed change record, corrected starter project, and conflict review

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
Review AI-assisted work within a bounded scope. Write evidence-based comments, apply targeted fixes, and make a human decision. The starter project includes deliberate defects for comparing human review and Copilot-assisted review.

Exercise Topic Time 1 Review a bounded change 30 min 2 Validate and correct the starter project 35 min 3 Resolve a conflict with review evidence 35 min 4 Evaluate review evidence and final decision 20 min

docs.title: Access and cost preflight
docs.text:
Read the course safety baseline. Before the lab, check the repository, synthetic data, reviewer, test command, and any usage limit.

Before you start, record these decisions in your notes:

  1. Repository scope: Are you using only lab/starter/review-project/, a private training fork, or an approved internal sandbox?
  2. Data boundary: Are all examples synthetic and allowed for review tooling?
  3. Review surface: Is Copilot review available?
  4. Required checks: Which command proves the starter project still works?
  5. Stop condition: What requires you to stop automated work?

Success criteria: You can explain what is allowed, what is out of scope, who reviews the work, and which check validates the change.

Learners need GitHub Copilot review, pull-request access, Git, Node.js, and npm. If any of these are unavailable, stop the lab. A local worksheet does not replace the pull-request and assisted-review practice.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Use these starter assets:

  • lab/starter/review-project/package.json: project scripts and dependencies
  • lab/starter/review-project/src/api.js: Express API under review
  • lab/starter/review-project/src/utils.js: utility functions under review
  • lab/starter/review-project/tests/api.test.js: existing Jest/Supertest checks
  • lab/starter/code-changes.md: intentionally flawed changes to review
  • lab/starter/partner-review-checklist.md: structured review worksheet
  • lab/starter/fix-evaluation-template.md: evidence template for corrected changes
  • lab/starter/conflict-scenario/README.md: manual merge-conflict scenario
  • lab/starter/conflict-scenario/utils-with-conflict.js: conflict exercise source file

Create a workspace outside the curriculum folder. This keeps the source materials unchanged:

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-07
cp -R lab/starter/review-project ~/copilot-labs/session-07/review-project
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-07/review-project
npm install
npm test

Expected: npm install completes without new dependencies and npm test reports that the existing API tests pass.

If install fails: Read package.json to find the expected test command. Record the error and continue with static review. Do not change package versions unless the instructor approves that troubleshooting exercise.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Review a bounded change (30 minutes)
Objective
docs.text: Review a deliberately flawed change set. Focus on risks you can connect to evidence and acceptance criteria.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the change brief. Read lab/starter/code-changes.md from start to finish.

Check: The brief lists changes to src/api.js and src/utils.js. Each has an intended defect.

  1. Create a review table in your notes. Use these columns:
Change Expected behavior Risk Evidence to inspect Review decision User search Safe filtering Injection risk query construction Request changes User list No sensitive fields data exposure response payload Request changes

Success criteria: Every row names a file or function to inspect before you comment.

  1. Inspect the current starter project before applying changes. Open src/api.js, src/utils.js, and tests/api.test.js.

Check: The baseline has a small API, utility functions, and existing tests. Record its behavior so you can separate existing code from introduced defects.

  1. Apply the change brief in a local branch or sandbox. In a Git repository, create a branch named feature/add-user-management. In a copied folder without Git, keep a written change log instead.

Success criteria: The modified files match the change brief closely enough for review; you have not added unrelated features.

  1. Run the existing checks.
npm test

Expected output: Some existing tests may still pass because the defects are not fully covered. Record both pass/fail output and any missing coverage you notice.

  1. Review the change yourself first. Use lab/starter/partner-review-checklist.md to record your initial verdict and the two findings that matter most before opening an assisted review.

Success criteria: Your initial review cites the relevant file or function and explains what evidence supports the verdict.

  1. Optional assisted review. After recording your own review, use Copilot review or an approved local agent when policy permits it. Ask it to review only the bounded change.

Suggested prompt:

Review only the changes described in code-changes.md. Focus on correctness,
security, tests, and whether the implementation should be approved.
Return file-specific findings with evidence. Do not propose unrelated rewrites.

Expected output: The assistant should produce specific findings. Note anything useful that you missed, reject unsupported findings, and record whether the new information changes your final decision.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
You are ready to continue when you can answer:

  • Which findings block approval?
  • Which findings are suggestions only?
  • Which defects were not covered by the existing tests?
  • What evidence would convince you that the fixes are complete?
  • What changed after the assisted review, if anything?

docs.title: Exercise 2: Validate and correct the starter project (35 minutes)
Objective
docs.text: Fix the defects with the smallest safe changes. Then show that the corrected project meets the review criteria.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Prioritize blocking findings. Start with issues that can leak sensitive data, allow injection, crash the server, or produce incorrect behavior.

Success criteria: Your fix plan lists each blocking defect, the target file, and the expected verification.

  1. Fix input handling in src/api.js. Replace unsafe string interpolation and fragile parsing with validated inputs and safe response shapes appropriate for the starter project.

Expected: The endpoint handles empty, missing, malformed, and valid inputs predictably. Tests or manual requests show the error responses.

  1. Fix sensitive response data. Ensure user-facing responses do not expose password-like or token-like fields.

Success criteria: Inspecting the JSON response shows only fields needed by the API contract.

  1. Fix pagination in src/utils.js. Verify that page 1 begins with the first item and boundary cases return predictable results.

Expected output: A focused test or manual Node.js check demonstrates page 1, page 2, and empty collections.

  1. Add or update focused tests in tests/api.test.js. Cover the behavior that was missing from the original test suite.

Success criteria: New tests fail before the fix and pass after the fix.

  1. Run checks again.
npm test

Expected output: All tests pass. If tests fail, record the failing assertion and correct only the related implementation or test expectation.

  1. Fill in lab/starter/fix-evaluation-template.md. Use it to summarize the finding, fix, test evidence, reviewer decision, and residual risk.

Success criteria: A reviewer can trace every fix back to an original finding.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2: fixes trace to findings
docs.text:
• Every blocking finding maps to a focused fix.
  • New tests cover the missed behavior.
  • npm test passes.
  • The fix evaluation names residual risk.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Resolve a merge conflict by preserving intent and adding verification. Do not blindly accept one side.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario. Open lab/starter/conflict-scenario/README.md.

You should observe: Two branches modify src/utils.js; one adds date formatting and the other changes price formatting.

  1. Open the conflicting source. Review lab/starter/conflict-scenario/utils-with-conflict.js.

Expected output: You can identify the conflicting region and state what each side is trying to accomplish.

  1. Write the desired merged behavior before editing. Use a short decision statement:
Preserve formatDate for date display and preserve formatPrice with an explicit
currency parameter. Existing callers should continue to work or be updated
intentionally.

Success criteria: Your statement names both branch intentions and the behavior that tests must prove.

  1. Resolve the conflict manually. Remove conflict markers, keep both valid behaviors, and avoid unrelated formatting changes.

Expected output: The file contains no <<<<<<<, =======, or >>>>>>> markers.

  1. Add focused tests. Verify date formatting, default currency behavior, explicit currency behavior, and any unchanged helper behavior.

Success criteria: Tests show that neither branch's intended behavior was lost.

  1. Run the project test command.

Expected output: The check passes and produces output you can use in the review.

  1. Peer review the resolution. Ask a partner to review only the conflict resolution and tests.

Success criteria: The reviewer can explain why both original branch goals are represented in the merged result.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3: conflict intent is preserved
docs.text:
• No conflict markers remain.
  • Both branch goals appear in the resolved behavior.
  • Tests cover date and currency formatting.
  • A peer can explain the merge decision from the record.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Make the final review decision from evidence, not an automated suggestion.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Select one blocking finding from Exercise 1. Choose a security, correctness, or reliability issue.

Success criteria: The finding includes a file reference, impact, and acceptance criterion.

  1. Record the fix evidence. Include before/after behavior, test names, and command output.

Expected output: A reviewer can reproduce the result from the recorded evidence.

  1. Classify remaining risk. Use these categories:
Risk type Question Data Did the change expose or process restricted data? Dependency Did the change add or update packages? Permission Did the workflow require a new permission? Security Did validation, error handling, or secrets handling change? Quality Are tests and review evidence sufficient?
  1. Write the final decision. Choose approve, request changes, or pause. Include the human reviewer and rationale.

Success criteria: The decision is understandable without seeing the entire lab conversation.

  1. Compare the locked independent critique with the assisted findings when applicable. Complete all comparison fields. Preserve the original critique, record which source raised each finding, and state why the final human assessment accepted, revised, or rejected it.

Expected output: The comparison table identifies differences, false positives, added evidence, and any finding that changed the final verdict.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4: final decision is evidence-based
docs.text:
• The decision is approve, request changes, or pause.
  • The rationale cites findings, fixes, and verification.
  • Automated findings were accepted only after human review.
  • Remaining risk and the reviewer are named.

docs.title: Final Deliverable
docs.text:
Submit one folder or document containing:

  1. The completed partner-review-checklist.md or equivalent review notes.
  2. A list of blocking findings and the smallest fix for each.
  3. Test evidence for the corrected project.
  4. The resolved conflict decision and validation evidence.
  5. A final human review decision: approve, request changes, or pause.

Done: A reviewer can reconstruct the original risk, fix, validation, and final decision without undocumented tool behavior.

docs.title: Verification checklist
docs.text:
• Findings are tied to evidence and acceptance criteria.
  • A human reviewer made the final decision.
  • Required checks were run.
  • Metered work stayed within the usage limit.
  • Starter files used: code-changes.md, partner-review-checklist.md, fix-evaluation-template.md, review-project/, and conflict-scenario/.

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session 07: Code Review Workflows
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Delivery baseline
docs.text: Read the course safety baseline. Before the demo, check the current GitHub docs and your organization's rules. Review controls and availability can change.

docs.title: Access and cost preflight
docs.text:
1. Choose the training repository, synthetic data, reviewer, and test command.
  2. Check the current docs for the review tools.
  3. Choose a small pull request with clear acceptance criteria.
  4. Set a usage limit if the work is metered.
  5. Check pull-request and Copilot review access before the lab.
  6. Ask learners to write their first verdict before assisted review.

docs.title: Access failure
docs.text: Stop the learner lab. The intentional defects can recover a trainer demonstration, but they do not replace pull-request and Copilot review practice.

docs.title: Session objective
docs.text: Teach automation as review input, not review authority. Learners check the diff, tests, and comments before making the decision.

docs.title: Suggested agenda
docs.text: Segment Activity Preflight Check data, roles, usage limits, and access. Review contract Define acceptance criteria and required checks. Findings Separate facts from assumptions. Human decision Accept, request changes, or reject with rationale. Conflict exercise Resolve intent and tests manually before editing. Access gate Stop when the required review surface is missing.

docs.title: Trainer talking points
docs.text:
"A review tool can raise questions, but it cannot replace the reviewer. The reviewer owns the decision and needs the diff and test results."

"Check the current workflow before the demo."

"For metered work, stop at the usage limit."

docs.title: Review contract
docs.text:
## Change intent
Describe the user-visible behavior and allowed scope.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Expected and failure behavior are testable.
- [ ] Relevant tests and checks pass.
- [ ] Data, dependencies, and permissions are reviewed.
- [ ] A human reviewer accepts the change.

docs.title: Review rubric
docs.text:
• Does the implementation meet the stated intent?
  • Do the tests cover the change?
  • Did the change introduce data, dependency, security, or permission questions?
  • Does the diff stay within the planned files?
  • Can the reviewer explain the decision to accept or request revision?

docs.title: Conflict-resolution exercise
docs.text: Have learners read both branch intentions, write the desired merged behavior, resolve the conflict manually, run tests, and review the result. An assisted demonstration is optional and may occur only when current documentation and policy permit it.

docs.title: Close
docs.text: Ask learners what they need to see before approving a change.

docs.title: Minute-mapped delivery plan (60 minutes)
docs.text: Time Segment Result 0:00 to 0:08 Review roles and accountability Author, automation, checks, and reviewer roles are named. 0:08 to 0:18 PR summaries and review contracts Learners separate generated prose from diff evidence. 0:18 to 0:28 Review requests and quality gates A policy-aware first-pass workflow is defined. 0:28 to 0:43 Scripted intentional-defect demo The group traces the finding, test, fix, and decision. 0:43 to 0:51 Suggested fixes and conflicts Learners preserve intent before editing. 0:51 to 0:58 Limits, adoption, and Q&A Learners design reversible human gates. 0:58 to 1:00 Close and lab handoff Reviewer roles and access are confirmed.

docs.title: Time-pressure cutpoints
docs.text:
• At 0:08, reduce lifecycle discussion to issue, diff, checks, and human decision.
  • At 0:18, draft only the Validation and Risk sections of the PR template.
  • At 0:28, describe automatic review governance without navigating settings.
  • At 0:38, use the prepared fix and focus on verification.
  • At 0:43, omit optional assisted fix application.
  • At 0:51, run the conflict decision statement without editing code.
  • Never cut human review, test output, access checks, or lab roles.

docs.title: Segment 1: Review is an accountable decision (0:00 to 0:08)
Trainer talking points
docs.text:
1. The author explains intent and supplies the diff and test output.
  2. Automated checks report configured results.
  3. An assisted review can surface hypotheses.
  4. A human reviewer evaluates intent, results, and risk.
  5. Branch rules and required approvals still apply.
  6. A generated summary, comment, or suggested fix is never proof by itself.
  7. Check current docs and organization rules before the demo.

docs.title: Opening prompt
docs.text:
Ask: "Who can explain why this change should merge?"

Expected answer: the author and reviewer, supported by the diff and test output.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Start with a review contract, not generated prose."

docs.title: Segment 2: Review contract and PR description (0:08 to 0:18)
Trainer walkthrough
docs.text:
Display:

## Problem
Suspended users must not view invoices.

## Change
Add an explicit suspended-status denial before role and ownership checks.

## Validation
- [ ] suspended administrator is denied
- [ ] suspended owner is denied
- [ ] active administrator is allowed
- [ ] active owner is allowed

## Risk and rollback
Authorization behavior changes only for suspended users; revert the bounded commit if needed.

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
• Compare every generated statement with the diff.
  • Do not claim a test ran unless command output exists.
  • Name breaking behavior, dependencies, permissions, and data implications.
  • Remove sensitive details from prose as well as code.
  • Keep the PR focused enough for a reviewer to reconstruct intent.
  • Use fictional examples; never use real organization names.

docs.title: Mini-exercise
docs.text:
Read: "Improves invoice security and all tests pass."

Ask learners to identify unsupported claims.

Expected response: "improves" needs defined behavior; "all tests pass" needs named command output.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Once the contract and evidence are ready, an assisted review can be requested as a first pass when approved."

docs.title: Segment 3: Review request and quality gates (0:18 to 0:28)
Exact preflight actions
docs.text:
1. Revisit the Delivery baseline.
  2. Confirm repository, data classification, author, reviewer, and required checks.
  3. Verify current official documentation for the selected review workflow.
  4. Check organization and repository rules.
  5. Set a usage limit and name who can approve more.
  6. Prepare the human-only review worksheet.
  7. Use a small synthetic diff.
  8. Check the review tool before opening it.

docs.title: Quality gates
docs.text: Gate Required result Ready for independent critique Clear intent, a small diff, and focused checks. Ready for assisted review The learner has written an initial verdict and the findings that matter most. Ready for human review Assisted comments, if any, are classified and checks reported. Ready for approval Acceptance criteria and risks are reviewed by an accountable human. Ready for merge Required approvals and repository protections are satisfied.

docs.title: Safe wording
docs.text:
"We demonstrate only the currently documented and approved controls. An assisted review is input to, not a replacement for, required reviewers."

Before the assisted prompt, have learners write their initial verdict and two important findings in lab/starter/partner-review-checklist.md. Afterward, they can compare missed findings, false positives, and anything that changed the final decision.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Now we will trace one defect from requirement to finding, test, fix, and decision."

docs.title: Scripted demo: Suspended invoice viewer (0:28 to 0:43)
Purpose
docs.text:
Show a complete review lifecycle using synthetic code and a localized authorization defect.

This example teaches review discipline. It does not prescribe production authorization design.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Use a disposable JavaScript file:

export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}

Requirement:

Suspended users must never view invoices.
Active administrators and active invoice owners may view an invoice.
Other users may not view it.

Prepare four fictional cases:

  • suspended administrator;
  • suspended owner;
  • active administrator;
  • unrelated active user.

docs.title: Exact assisted-review prompt
docs.text:
When current access and policy permit:

Review only canViewInvoice against the stated requirement.
Return one file-specific finding with observed behavior, impact, and a test idea.
Do not propose unrelated refactoring.

docs.title: Exact trainer actions
docs.text:
1. Read the requirement before the implementation.
  2. Ask learners to predict each case.
  3. Run a prepared test or trace the cases manually.
  4. If approved, request the bounded assisted review.
  5. Classify the response as valid, uncertain, noise, or out of scope.
  6. Restate the valid finding:
Observed: suspended administrators and owners currently return true.
Required: suspended users must always return false.
Decision: request changes and add regression coverage.
  1. Add or display a failing suspended-administrator test.
  2. Apply the smallest proposed fix:
export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  if (user.status === "suspended") return false;
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}
  1. Run all four focused cases.
  2. Inspect the complete diff.
  3. Ask the human reviewer to choose approve, request changes, or pause.

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text:
• The pre-fix suspended cases demonstrate the defect.
  • The post-fix suspended cases return false.
  • Active administrator behavior remains true.
  • An unrelated active user remains denied.
  • The diff contains one guard plus focused test changes.
  • The final decision cites requirement and test evidence.

docs.title: Verification prompts
docs.text:
• Does the guard run before role and ownership checks?
  • Is the status value defined by the fictional contract?
  • Did any unrelated behavior change?
  • Which test failed before and passed after?
  • Does the review comment distinguish observation from assumption?

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
Give learners the requirement, original function, and truth-table rows.

They complete:

User state Role/ownership Before Required Decision Suspended Admin true false Block Suspended Owner true false Block Active Admin true true Preserve Active Neither false false Preserve

Learners write a review comment, minimal patch, and test names on the worksheet.

A peer makes the final decision.

Use this only to recover the trainer demonstration. Learners still need the required review surfaces for the lab.

docs.title: Demo recovery
docs.text:
• If the assisted review misses the defect, use the worksheet to finish the trainer explanation.
  • If it invents broader policy, mark the comment uncertain or out of scope.
  • If tests cannot run, stop the learner lab and fix the environment.
  • If a suggested fix rewrites unrelated code, reject it and use the guard only.
  • If review access fails during the demo, use the worksheet and fix access before the lab.
  • If the run reaches its usage limit, stop assisted activity and record progress.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Applying a fix saved typing at most; the requirement, regression test, and human decision made it reviewable."

docs.title: Segment 5: Suggested fixes and conflict intent (0:43 to 0:51)
Before applying any suggested fix
docs.text:
1. Restate the finding independently.
  2. Reproduce the defect or locate the violated criterion.
  3. Inspect the entire patch.
  4. Add a test that fails before the fix when practical.
  5. Run broader checks proportional to risk.
  6. Retain author ownership and human review.

docs.title: Conflict micro-exercise
docs.text:
Present:

Branch A adds formatDate.
Branch B adds an explicit currency parameter to formatPrice.

Before editing, learners write:

Preserve date formatting and price formatting with explicit currency.
Keep existing callers working or update them intentionally.

Ask for four checks:

  • no conflict markers;
  • date example;
  • default currency example;
  • explicit currency example.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Review assistance has limits, so keep human review and an off switch."

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
Assisted review may help surface localized correctness, missing tests, error handling, or convention mismatches.

It may miss unstated product intent, cross-system behavior, subtle authorization issues, operational risk, or misleading but plausible changes.

Start with a small repository set.

Measure actionable findings, noise, rework, delays, and escaped defects.

Assign an owner for triage and escalation.

Expand only when the organization's quality and risk criteria are met.

Keep a documented disable or pause decision.

docs.title: "Can Copilot approve a PR?"
docs.text: Do not treat an assisted response as accountable approval. Follow current repository rules, required reviewers, and organizational policy.

docs.title: "Should we apply every suggested fix?"
docs.text: No. Reproduce the issue, inspect the complete patch, add a focused test, and accept only the smallest correct change.

docs.title: "What if human and assisted reviews disagree?"
docs.text: Return to the requirements, diff, and test output. The reviewer records the decision or asks a domain owner.

docs.title: "Can automatic review replace branch protection?"
docs.text: Do not bypass required controls. Check the current configuration and keep the required human review.

docs.title: "Why review a generated PR description?"
docs.text: It can invent results, omit risk, or misread intent. Compare every claim with the diff and command output.

docs.title: "Is security review covered by this feature?"
docs.text: An assisted general review is not a substitute for the organization's required security practices, tooling, or specialists.

docs.title: "Which repositories should enable automatic review?"
docs.text: That is an organization decision. Start with a few low-risk repositories and define exclusions, owners, measures, and a way to disable the feature.

docs.title: "How is review activity priced or metered?"
docs.text: Check current docs and organization terms. Do not teach static prices or allowances.

docs.title: Pitfalls, anti-patterns, and recoveries
docs.text: Anti-pattern Recovery Reviewing the summary before the diff Read intent, diff, and checks first. Treating comments as findings without proof Reproduce the issue or tie the comment to a criterion. Applying a patch from the highlighted lines only Inspect the entire proposed patch. Approving because checks are green Review coverage, intent, risk, and scope. Blindly choosing "ours" in a conflict Write merged behavior before editing. Mixing style noise with blockers Classify severity and approval impact. Claiming tests passed without output Name and rerun the relevant command. Using restricted PR data in an unapproved flow Stop and use the synthetic local exercise. Removing required human review Restore repository gates and escalate. Assuming fixed UI or availability Check current docs before delivery.

docs.title: Closing script
docs.text: "Automation can broaden a first pass, but the reviewer owns the decision. A useful review connects intent, the diff, test output, the smallest correction, and the reviewer's rationale."

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Open lab/README.md.

Assign author and reviewer roles.

Learners use code-changes.md, partner-review-checklist.md, fix-evaluation-template.md, the local review project, and the conflict scenario.

The worksheet supports the prepared trainer demonstration. It does not replace the learner pull-request workflow.

docs.title: Readiness checklist
docs.text:
• A small synthetic change is selected.
  • Required checks and reviewer are named.
  • Pull-request and Copilot review access is available.
  • Findings will name the file and function.
  • The conflict intent statement is ready.
  • A usage limit is recorded when it applies.
  • Final approval remains a human decision.

docs.title: Session 08: Copilot App, Plugins & Canvas Extensions
docs.text:
Launch Slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Agentic Workflows

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions 01 to 07

Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hours lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This session teaches canvas extension design through one synthetic delivery-readiness board. Learners define the contract first, create the canvas in the GitHub Copilot app when access is approved, test direct and agent-requested updates, force a safe rejection, recover, and inspect the final canvas against the contract.

A canvas is a shared interactive surface. People use visible controls while an agent uses named capabilities against the same state. The canvas does not replace the system that owns the work.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Choose a canvas only when visible shared state improves the workflow.
  • Separate canvas state, human actions, and agent-callable capabilities.
  • Write validation rules that reject unsafe or incomplete state changes.
  • Create and review a project-scoped or user-scoped canvas.
  • Recover from a rejected action without weakening the contract.
  • Record ownership, review, failure handling, and retirement decisions.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
Learners submit:

  1. a completed canvas contract;
  2. a canvas created in an approved sandbox;
  3. checkpoint evidence for direct, agent-requested, rejected, and recovered changes;
  4. a final state that matches the contract.

docs.title: Access policy
docs.text:
The lab requires GitHub Copilot app access and the built-in /create-canvas skill. Project scope also requires approval to create files under .github/extensions.

If app access or /create-canvas is unavailable, stop the lab. If project scope is unavailable, use user scope. Do not bypass policy or install a replacement.

docs.title: Session materials
docs.text:
Resource Purpose trainer-content/README.md Minute-mapped teaching and demo plan slides.md Trainer-facing teaching deck lab/README.md Two-hour learner guide lab/starter/ Prepared inputs and contract harness lab/solution/ Worked contract, final state, and completed evidence

The default lab remains the delivery-readiness board. An optional Feature Workbench variant uses synthetic CI results to practice a test-gate decision:

  • lab/starter/feature-workbench-contract.md
  • lab/starter/feature-workbench-sample.json
  • lab/solution/feature-workbench-solution.md
  • lab/solution/feature-workbench-final-state.json

See the curriculum glossary for canvas, capability, plugin, and MCP terminology.

docs.text:
